meta.title: NZ Politics 2026: What they actually said

facts: Saturday 7 November 2026. Prime Minister Christopher Luxon announced the date on 21 January 2026.
Runs from Monday 26 October to Friday 6 November 2026. Voting is in person (online voting only for overseas voters).
Reported to close at midnight on Sunday 25 October 2026, and you cannot enrol at a voting place. Uncertain: the Vote.nz key-dates page blocked our fetch, so please check it at vote.nz.
The 54th Parliament was dissolved on 1 October 2026. Ministers stay in office until a new government is formed.
This will not be held with the 2026 election. The government dropped the planned referendum on 18 February 2026 (secondary source: Wikipedia).

context: The current government is the Sixth National Government, formed in November 2023. National leads it with two separate coalition agreements, one with ACT and one with NZ First. Winston Peters was Deputy Prime Minister until 31 May 2025, when David Seymour took over under the agreed rotation.
Seats at dissolution: National 49, ACT 11 and NZ First 8 (government total 68). Labour 34, Greens 15, Te Pāti Māori 4 and two independents (both former Te Pāti Māori MPs). That is 123 seats in total.

Polls in the final month show both major parties well below their 2023 results. The 6 October RNZ–Reid Research poll put National and Labour together at 56.7%, down from 64.9% at the 2023 election. Neither the current coalition nor a Labour–Green–Te Pāti Māori bloc has a clear majority in these polls, and the Opportunity Party (outside Parliament) is often the kingmaker. Luxon has ruled out working with Opportunity.

Big issues of 2026: the cost of living (made worse by a fuel-price spike linked to the 2026 Middle East conflict); tax (Labour's capital gains tax, the Greens' wealth taxes, National's 'no new taxes' pledge); two challenges to Luxon's leadership inside National (April and August); the law replacing the RMA, passed in September; Treaty and Waitangi Tribunal policy; immigration; and turmoil inside Te Pāti Māori.
meta.other_parties_note: Te Tai Tokerau Party was founded in May 2026 by Mariameno Kapa-Kingi, the sitting MP for Te Tai Tokerau, after her split from Te Pāti Māori. Its list has two names (Kyla Campbell-Kamariera and Kapa-Kingi). It is not profiled in depth here. It is listed because 1News counts it in the left bloc's seat projections if Kapa-Kingi holds her seat.

parties.name: New Zealand National Party
parties.selection: The leader plus list places 2 to 5 on National's 2026 list (released 8 August 2026): deputy leader Nicola Willis (2), Chris Bishop (3), Simeon Brown (4) and Erica Stanford (5). All four are senior Cabinet ministers.
parties.history: Founded in 1936 from a merger of the United and Reform parties. It is New Zealand's main centre-right party and has led governments under Holland, Holyoake, Muldoon, Bolger/Shipley and Key/English. It won the most votes in 2023 and formed the current government with ACT and NZ First.
parties.ideology: Centre-right. Liberal-conservative, pro-market, and focused on fiscal restraint, law and order, and 'getting the basics right'.
parties.role: Leads the Sixth National Government (since 27 November 2023) under separate coalition agreements with ACT and NZ First. Christopher Luxon is Prime Minister and Nicola Willis is Minister of Finance.
policies: 'No new taxes': on 23 August 2026 Luxon widened the pledge from 'no new taxes on working people' and ruled out a bank tax and a bed (accommodation) tax.
https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics_election-2026/1083119/national-promises-no-new-taxes-if-re-elected
Welfare: Jobseeker changes announced 8 October 2026, including random drug testing ('If you can work, you should').
https://x.com/chrisluxonmp/status/2107949741086765497
Education: NCEA to be replaced by new qualifications (NZCE at Year 12, NZACE at Year 13). Details were confirmed in May 2026.
https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics/595424/government-confirms-ncea-replacement-details
Planning: the Planning Act and Natural Environment Act replacing the RMA passed on 22 September 2026. The full system is intended to be running by 2030.
https://www.national.org.nz/news/260922-chrisbishop
Social media: a bill to ban under-16s from most social media platforms was introduced as a National Party bill in August 2026. ACT and NZ First oppose it (secondary source).
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sixth_National_Government_of_New_Zealand

Fiscal plan (12 October 2026): tax relief only once the books are back in surplus (not forecast before 2029); a commitment to an independent election policy-costing unit by the 2029 election; $451.8m to extend the school lunch programme to the next election.
https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics_election-2026/1858565/national-hints-at-tax-cuts-after-2029-as-fiscal-plan-released

Superannuation: National confirmed its fiscal plan is its super policy. It still proposes raising the age gradually but sets no date, and commits to cross-party talks within 100 days of a new government.
https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics_election-2026/1860419/politicians-can-t-dance-alone-on-superannuation-nicola-willis
Aid: a plan to cut aid outside the Pacific to fund health spending. Coalition partner NZ First publicly criticised it.
https://x.com/winstonpeters/status/2107229536366850450
events: April 2026: after media reports of caucus discontent, Luxon called a confidence vote on his own leadership and won it (21 April). A reshuffle earlier that month moved the campaign-chair role from Chris Bishop to Simeon Brown.
https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics/592984/prime-minister-christopher-luxon-survives-confidence-vote
August 2026: Chris Penk challenged Luxon. Luxon survived a second confidence vote on 12 August and stripped Penk of his portfolios. Penk later withdrew as a candidate.
https://www.1news.co.nz/2026/08/12/pm-wins-leadership-vote-after-challenge-fails-penk-wont-seek-re-election/

https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics_election-2026/1311337/asa-partly-upholds-complaint-against-misleading-national-attack-ad
Budget 2026 (28 May) was billed as restrained. Willis said she had not convinced coalition partners to raise the NZ Super age.
https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics/596665/just-need-to-vote-for-it-nicola-willis-ends-budget-speech-with-call-to-arms-for-supporters
Luxon has ruled out working with the Opportunity Party, and has called strategic vote-splitting 'insanely stupid'.
https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics_election-2026/1749693/rnz-reid-research-poll-national-crashes-greens-surge-opportunity-kingmaker

parties.name: The Opportunity Party (formerly TOP)

people.name: Christopher Luxon
people.role: Prime Minister; Leader of the National Party; Minister for National Security and Intelligence
people.seat: MP for Botany (since 2020); contesting Botany
people.background: Former chief executive of Air New Zealand and a former Unilever executive. Entered Parliament in 2020, became National leader in November 2021 and Prime Minister in November 2023.
positions: 'No new taxes' (no bank tax, no bed tax); tough welfare obligations, including drug testing for Jobseekers.
Has ruled out working with the Opportunity Party because of its land value tax; calls vote-splitting 'insanely stupid'.
Campaigns on economic 'turnaround' and 'fixing the basics'.
reversals: National's tax pledge was originally 'no new taxes on working people'. In August 2026 Luxon widened it to 'no new taxes', dropping a bank tax and bed tax that ministers (including Willis) had floated earlier in the year.

In early May 2026 Luxon said National would 'go to the election with another election policy around superannuation and lifting the retirement age for sure'. Its 12 October fiscal plan set no date for raising the age and committed to cross-party talks instead. National says its stance has not changed.

quotes.text: It requires a political consensus, and we don't have that currently.
quotes.context: Explaining why National's superannuation policy is cross-party talks rather than a set date for raising the age (reported by RNZ)

quotes.text: We want to work with parties that want no new taxes. It's as simple as that.
quotes.context: Holding to his rule-out of working with the Opportunity Party, citing its land value tax.

quotes.text: It's absolute madness.
quotes.context: On RNZ Morning Report, responding to NZ First's policy of buying back BNZ (said 'that's just not going to happen').

quotes.text: I just wrapped up my campaign launch speech, and my message was simple: Where do you want your hard-earned money going, to you and your family, or to Labour and their mates? Party Vote National for no new taxes.
quotes.context: X post after National's campaign launch at the Auckland Convention Centre.

quotes.text: There was a confidence vote in my leadership this morning at our caucus meeting, and I have the full support of our caucus. And our caucus is united, and it is determined to win this election.
quotes.context: After surviving a second caucus confidence vote in four months, triggered by Chris Penk's challenge.

quotes.text: I have the support of my caucus as their leader. Caucus has answered clearly and decisively. It has backed my leadership, and that matter is now closed.
quotes.context: After forcing a caucus confidence vote on his own leadership amid media reports of discontent.

quotes.text: Kiwis expect the media to ask us the tough questions about our policies... They are not interested in the media soap opera.
quotes.context: Same statement after the April confidence vote.

quotes.text: We've been doing a big turnaround, we've been fixing a lot of the basics. We now have an opportunity, as this recovery comes through, not just to watch it come through but to actually shape the future of this country...
quotes.context: Election-date announcement; pitching National's economic record.

quotes.context: On NZ Super, the day National confirmed its fiscal plan was its superannuation policy (cross-party talks, no set date for raising the age)

quotes.text: I have looked at what the banks are being taxed at now and measures for changing that, and there are no other measures that I can see won't result in additional costs for Kiwis.
quotes.context: Explaining why National dropped a bank tax under its 'no new taxes' pledge.

quotes.text: It's a Budget that does what's right for the country... this is not a time to be getting us further into the hock, to be whacking another set of bills on the credit card.
quotes.context: RNZ Morning Report, asked whether a restrained Budget was risky in election year.

quotes.text: I will go to the campaign trail as the National Party finance spokesperson with my view on what would be appropriate, well signalled, fair, transparent, gradual, gradual changes to New Zealand superannuation.
quotes.context: Post-Budget, on NZ Super costs rising; she added: "I haven't been able to convince my coalition partners yet, but I retain hope."

quotes.text: New Zealand is digging its way out of the post-Covid hole.
quotes.context: Delivering Budget 2026.

quotes.text: We've got to make sure the banks are taxed fairly... As a minister in this Government, I am still actively considering the taxation of banks and what that looks like.
quotes.context: May 2026 comments (exact day not given in source), as quoted by 1News when she later dropped the idea.

quotes.text: One for all, all for one. And when the caucus, by majority, have confidence in the leader, then we all stand together, backing the leader.
quotes.context: As deputy leader, after Luxon survived the April caucus confidence vote.

people.name: Chris Bishop
people.role: Attorney-General (since April 2026); Minister of Housing; Infrastructure; Transport; RMA Reform
people.seat: MP for Hutt South; contesting Hutt South

quotes.text: I will consider the reforms to have failed.
quotes.context: Newsroom interview: if, in five years, the new planning system has not made the fast-track regime unnecessary.

quotes.text: Passing these Bills is not the end of the job. The next task is making sure the new system works in practice.

quotes.text: I think what the Prime Minister was saying, which I would broadly agree with, is that the country has very difficult challenges ahead of it and we should spend our time focused on those challenges.

quotes.text: Obviously I love being the campaign chair, and it's a role I enjoy doing, but it's fine - I've got plenty of things to do.
quotes.context: After losing the campaign-chair and Leader of the House roles in the April reshuffle while becoming Attorney-General.

people.name: Simeon Brown
people.role: Minister of Health; Minister for Energy; State Owned Enterprises; National campaign chair (since April 2026)
people.seat: MP for Pakuranga (since 2017); contesting Pakuranga

quotes.context: Responding after the ASA partly upheld a complaint that a National attack ad on Labour's CGT was misleading.

quotes.context: LinkedIn post on becoming campaign chair.

quotes.text: These changes are about ensuring treatments are safe and carefully managed, while maintaining access to care for those who need it.
quotes.context: As Health Minister, announcing a pause on new puberty-blocker prescriptions for gender dysphoria pending a UK trial.

people.name: Erica Stanford
people.role: Minister of Education; Minister of Immigration; lead minister on the Royal Commission (abuse in care) response

quotes.text: We want young people leaving school with qualifications that are clear, rigorous and widely understood by parents, employers, tertiary providers and students themselves.
quotes.context: National Party release on the NCEA replacement.

people.name: Chris Hipkins
people.role: Leader of the Labour Party; Leader of the Opposition

people.name: Carmel Sepuloni
people.role: Deputy Leader of the Labour Party

quotes.context: First-reading debate on the move-on orders bill, which she called "purely ideological".

quotes.context: Same interview, on whether income-tax changes are possible once in surplus.

quotes.context: Same release.

quotes.context: Same address, on foreign policy.

quotes.context: Launching the Greens' tax package (wealth, inheritance and corporate taxes; income-tax cuts for 96%).

quotes.context: Same address.
